cards.explanation: The answer is that the foolish woman tears her house down with her own hands. The proverb says "Every wise woman builds her house, but a foolish one tears it down with her own hands." The wise woman builds her house. The foolish one tears hers down, friends, and she does it with her own hands.

The answer is True. The man who walks in uprightness fears the LORD, "…but the one who is devious in his ways despises Him." Two men, two directions, and the text puts the LORD right in the middle of the contrast.

The answer is a rod to his back. The verse says "The proud speech of a fool brings a rod to his back…" His own mouth sends the bill. The same verse says the lips of the wise protect them, so a mouth can be a shield or a problem, depending on whose it is.

The word is harvest. The verse says "Where there are no oxen, the manger is empty, but an abundant harvest comes through the strength of the ox." No oxen means an empty manger. The harvest is what comes through the ox's strength, friends.

The answer is that he finds none. The text says "A mocker seeks wisdom and finds none…" He goes looking and comes back with empty hands. Meanwhile, "…knowledge comes easily to the discerning." Easy for one, none for the other.

The answer is False. The proverb says, "Stay away from a foolish man; you will gain no knowledge from his speech." No knowledge, not a little, not eventually. Save your listening time, friends, for somebody who has something to teach.

The answer is that his folly deceives him. The verse says "The wisdom of the prudent is to discern his way, but the folly of fools deceives them." So the prudent man discerns his way, and the fool gets deceived by his own folly. Getting fooled by your own folly is a rough way to get got.

The answer is a stranger. The verse says "…no stranger shares in its joy." The heart knows its own bitterness, and it also has joys that an outsider can't fully enter. I think that's why it helps to have people close enough to be more than strangers.

The answer is False. The verse says "The house of the wicked will be destroyed, but the tent of the upright will flourish." So the wicked man's house is the one that comes down, friends. The upright man's tent is the one that flourishes.

The answer is True. The verse says "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death." It's a heavy line, and I'll let it be heavy. A way can seem right, and the verse still tells you where it ends.

The answer is False. The verse says "Even in laughter the heart may ache, and joy may end in sorrow." Laughing and hurting can happen at the same time, friends. So if somebody's laughing, I think it's worth being kind anyway.
The word is rewarded. The verse says "…a good man is rewarded for his ways." The backslider gets the fill of his own ways, and the good man gets rewarded for his. Each one gets what his ways bring.

The answer is that the simple man believes every word. The proverb says "The simple man believes every word, but the prudent man watches his steps." The simple man takes in every word, friends. The prudent man is busy watching his steps.
The word is careless. The verse says "…a fool is careless and reckless." Careless and reckless, a two-for-one. The wise man, meanwhile, "…fears and turns from evil…"

The first blank is foolishly, and the second is hated. The proverb says "A quick-tempered man acts foolishly, and a devious man is hated." A short fuse gets its label right there in the verse. And hated is the word the verse gives the devious man, friends. Sneaky doesn't win people over, I'd say.

The answer is False. The verse says "The evil bow before the good, and the wicked at the gates of the righteous." The evil are the ones who bow before the good, friends. So the bowing runs the other way.

The answer is the rich man. The verse says "…many are those who love the rich." The proverb is describing how things go, and it's a hard one. The poor man is "…hated even by his neighbor…" It doesn't say that's how it should be.

The answer is True. The verse says "…blessed is he who shows kindness to the poor." It comes right after "He who despises his neighbor sins…" Two choices, friends, and the proverb says which one is blessed.

The answer is loving devotion and faithfulness. The verse says "…those who plan goodness find loving devotion and faithfulness." Planning goodness is the work, and devotion and faithfulness are what they find. The ones who contrive evil, the verse says, go astray.
The answer is False. The proverb says "There is profit in all labor, but mere talk leads only to poverty." Notice it says all labor. Talking about the work isn't doing the work, friends.

The answer is True. The proverb says "He who fears the LORD is secure in confidence, and his children shall have a place of refuge." The man who fears the LORD is secure in confidence, friends. His children shall have a place of refuge.

The answer is the snares of death. The fear of the LORD is "…a fountain of life, turning a man from the snares of death." It gives life and it turns him away from snares. Both halves are in one verse.

The word is ruin. The proverb says "A large population is a king’s splendor, but a lack of subjects is a prince’s ruin." Splendor goes with a large population, friends. Ruin goes with a lack of subjects.
The answer is False. The proverb says "A patient man has great understanding…" Patient and slow aren't the same thing, friends. It's the quick-tempered man who "promotes folly."
The answer is envy. The verse says "…envy rots the bones." It sets that right beside "A tranquil heart is life to the body…" It's an ugly word for an ugly thing, friends.

The word is taunts. The verse says "Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker…" The proverb ties how a person treats the poor to the One who made them. And the same verse says "…whoever is kind to the needy honors Him."

The answer is even in death. The verse says "The wicked man is thrown down by his own sin, but the righteous man has a refuge even in death." Even in death, the verse says, friends. That's the part to hold onto.

The first blank is exalts, and the second is disgrace. The proverb says "Righteousness exalts a nation…" It lifts a nation up. And it goes on, "…sin is a disgrace to any people." Righteousness exalts a nation, friends, and sin is a disgrace to any people.

The answer is his anger. The verse says "A king delights in a wise servant, but his anger falls on the shameful." The wise servant gets the king's delight, friends. The shameful get his anger, and I know which one I'd rather get.
